SOURCE AUDITThe slides constitute PDF pages 1–55; the professor’s written handout begins on PDF page 56. Course terminology and slides control the main narrative. Conflicting statements are visibly flagged rather than silently reconciled. First Aid content has been explicitly marked.
Learning objective 1

Neurons, neuroglia and the PNS: a histologic orientation

The central nervous system comprises brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system consists of nerve fibers and peripheral neuronal cell bodies in ganglia, communicating between the CNS and peripheral tissues. A neuron is the electrically signaling cell; a glial cell provides structural, metabolic, insulating, homeostatic or immune support. In an H&E section, neurons are typically conspicuous because their cell bodies are large, have an open/euchromatic nucleus with a prominent nucleolus, and often show basophilic Nissl substance. The small, dense nuclei scattered nearby commonly belong to glia.

Neuropil is the intricate mesh of dendrites, axons, synapses, supporting glial processes and small vessels between CNS neuronal somata. It looks like a fine fibrillary background rather than a collagen-based connective-tissue matrix. Remember the location-based naming rule: a cluster of neuron somata is a ganglion in the PNS, generally a nucleus in the CNS; bundles of axons are nerves in the PNS and tracts in the CNS.

For PNS glia, distinguish satellite cells, which wrap and support neuron cell bodies in ganglia, from Schwann cells, which ensheath peripheral axons and may form myelin. This is the essential starting distinction for later images of ganglia versus peripheral nerves.

MUST KNOWNeuron soma: large, often pale nucleus and prominent nucleolus. Satellite cell: small peripheral nucleus around ganglion soma. Schwann cell: supports an axon. Neuropil: fine neuroglial meshwork, not ordinary connective tissue.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINTWhat features tell you that a stained large cell is a neuron rather than a glial cell?
Reveal answerAn enlarged cell body with an open nucleus, conspicuous nucleolus and often cytoplasmic Nissl substance, contrasted with smaller, dark glial nuclei.
Learning objective 2

Neuronal polarity, neuron types and synapses (including the motor end plate)

The cell body, dendrites and axon

The soma / perikaryon is the chief synthetic and metabolic compartment: abundant rough ER (aggregated Nissl bodies), free ribosomes and Golgi apparatus maintain proteins needed throughout the neuron. Dendrites branch extensively to receive and integrate inputs, often via specialized dendritic spines. The single axon carries a propagated action potential toward a synaptic terminal. The pale axon hillock and proximal axon lack Nissl bodies, an important practical histology clue. The handout identifies the initial segment, just beyond the hillock, as the typical site of action-potential initiation because of its abundance of voltage-gated channels.

Identify three structural classes

TypeProcessesTypical location / role
MultipolarOne axon and multiple dendritesMost frequent; motor neurons and many CNS interneurons
BipolarOne axon + one dendritic processSpecial sensory pathways, including retina, olfactory and vestibular connections
PseudounipolarSingle stem process bifurcating into peripheral and central branchesDorsal-root and many cranial sensory ganglia; primary afferent neurons

A pseudounipolar sensory neuron conducts impulses from its peripheral process toward its central process without a conventional synapse in the dorsal-root ganglion. Be careful: its apparent “single process” distinguishes it from true unipolar neurons, which the lecturer notes are more typical in invertebrates.

Synaptic structure: identify it on electron microscopy

Chemical synapse: presynaptic axon bouton containing small, electron-lucent synaptic vesicles and mitochondria → narrow synaptic cleft → postsynaptic membrane concentrated in transmitter receptors. Ca²⁺-dependent exocytosis releases neurotransmitter; transmitter molecules bind to receptors on the receiving cell (the vesicles themselves are not taken up by the postsynaptic membrane as the key signaling mechanism). Electrical synapses instead use gap junctions for very rapid direct ionic communication. The slides also distinguish axodendritic, axosomatic and axoaxonic sites.

Neuromuscular junction (NMJ) and motor unit

The motor end plate is a specialized chemical synapse where a somatic motor axon contacts a skeletal muscle fiber. Terminal branches of the motor axon release acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft. The muscle sarcolemma forms folded junctional / secondary clefts, concentrating acetylcholine receptors; acetylcholinesterase in the cleft terminates signaling. The motor axon and all the muscle fibers it supplies together form a motor unit. A small motor unit supports precision; a larger motor unit supports powerful gross movements.

DON’T MIX THESE UPAxon hillock = pale, Nissl-negative initiation region; dendrite = Nissl may extend into it; motor end plate = specialized muscle postsynaptic membrane, not the entire motor unit.
MSK CONNECTIONLecture 3 covered threshold and voltage-gated action potentials. This histology lecture identifies the compartments and specialized junction where those signals are generated and converted into skeletal-muscle excitation.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINTIn an EM image, what three features establish that a structure is a chemical synapse?
Reveal answerA vesicle-rich presynaptic bouton, a synaptic cleft, and a specialized postsynaptic membrane containing transmitter receptors.
Learning objective 3

Schwann cells, myelin, unmyelinated fibers and peripheral nerve coverings

How a Schwann cell forms peripheral myelin

A peripheral axon sinks into a Schwann-cell groove; the membrane folds meet to produce a mesaxon. Repeated wrapping of Schwann plasma membrane forms concentric layers, whose cytoplasm becomes compressed/excluded during compaction. The resulting sheath is lipid-rich (approximately 70% lipid) and appears as an optically clear or white halo in H&E because lipids are dissolved by routine processing. One Schwann cell forms one myelinated internode of one axon; an entire long axon has many sequential Schwann cells. The short exposed gaps between internodes are the nodes of Ranvier, which cluster voltage-gated channels and permit saltatory conduction.

Unmyelinated PNS axons are not “naked.” Schwann cell cytoplasm encloses them, but its membrane does not spiral repeatedly to form compact myelin. Multiple small axons can be housed in Schwann-cell invaginations (a Remak bundle; terminology added for orientation). Their impulses are propagated continuously, so conduction is slower than in otherwise comparable myelinated fibers.

Identify peripheral nerve layers under H&E

SheathWhat it surroundsAppearance and function
EndoneuriumIndividual myelinated axon/Schwann unit or small groups of nonmyelinated axonsFine, vascular loose connective tissue between axonal profiles
PerineuriumEach axon bundle / fascicleDistinct concentric epithelial-like barrier layer; blood–nerve barrier
EpineuriumEntire nerve, comprising multiple fasciclesDense irregular connective tissue; larger vessels and possible adipose tissue

At low power, find the whole nerve boundary first (epineurium), then identify rounded fascicles and their perineurial rings, then zoom into endoneurial axon-and-myelin circles. Longitudinal sections show wavy fibers with long Schwann-cell nuclei and occasional constrictions at nodes of Ranvier. Cross-sections of myelinated fibers resemble pale circular “donuts” because their myelin has been extracted.

EXAM TRAP · SOURCE DISCREPANCYSlide 23 explains that more than one unmyelinated axon may occupy a Schwann-cell channel; the handout (PDF page 63) says “one Schwann cell associates with only one axon” in the nonmyelinated discussion. That handout sentence conflicts with the slide and its own description elsewhere. For this Companion, preserve the discrepancy and use the illustrated multiple-axon arrangement to recognize unmyelinated PNS fibers.
FIRST AID CONNECTIONFirst Aid 2025 (neurology anatomy/physiology) emphasizes that perineurium is the blood–nerve barrier, and contrasts Schwann cells (PNS) with oligodendrocytes (CNS).
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINTWhere is the perineurium in a routine H&E nerve section—and why is a bright white ring around an axon not a node of Ranvier?
Reveal answerPerineurium encircles an entire fascicle. A pale round ring in cross-section is extracted myelin; a node of Ranvier is a short interruption along the length of a myelinated axon.
Learning objective 4

Axonal transport: maintaining distant terminals

Many peripheral axons extend far from their soma, but the main protein-synthesis machinery is concentrated in the cell body. Their terminals must therefore be supplied continuously, while signals about the target and damaged organelles must return to the soma. This is accomplished by vesicle and organelle traffic along microtubule tracks inside the axon.

DirectionMotorCargo and significance
Anterograde: soma → distal axon/terminalKinesinSynaptic-vesicle components, enzymes, membrane proteins, organelles including mitochondria
Retrograde: terminal → somaDyneinTarget-derived growth factors / neurotrophic signals, spent vesicular material, damaged organelles and certain pathogens

Reasoning chain: loss of axonal transport → inadequate synaptic machinery at distal terminal OR inability to deliver survival signals back to soma → progressive malfunction, especially in long axons. The transport direction is defined relative to the cell body, not the direction of a particular sensory or motor impulse.

MUST KNOWKinesin carries anterograde cargo; dynein carries retrograde cargo. Motor proteins move physical cargo, not action potentials. The lecture explicitly includes growth factors traveling retrograde.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINTWhich route lets a distal nerve ending inform the neuronal soma that its target tissue is healthy?
Reveal answerRetrograde, dynein-associated transport of growth or neurotrophic signals to the soma.
Learning objective 5

Peripheral nerve injury, Wallerian degeneration, regeneration and neuropathy

What happens when a peripheral axon is injured?

The portion of axon distal to a sufficiently severe lesion disconnects from the cell body and undergoes Wallerian degeneration. The distal axon breaks into irregular fragments; its myelin sheath splits into lipid-rich myelin ovoids, giving the section a fragmented/vacuolated appearance. Macrophages and Schwann cells remove axon and myelin debris. The injured soma may show chromatolysis (loss/dispersal of Nissl substance, swollen cell body, peripheral nuclear displacement)—a repair response, not the same as Wallerian degeneration at the distal stump.

If the neuronal cell body survives and the path back to the target remains permissive, the proximal axon sends out new growth cones. Repair-state Schwann cells proliferate and align as Bands of Büngner, guiding axonal extension through preserved basal lamina/endoneurial tubes. Reconnections can restore function. Failed fascicular alignment, long target distance, extensive crush/transection and atrophied target tissue may leave disordered regrowth and permanent impairment. The course diagram contrasts successful versus unsuccessful reinnervation.

Two tissue injury patterns

Axonal neuropathyDemyelinating neuropathy
Primary loss or degeneration of axon; myelin may be secondarily lostPrimary damage to myelin/Schwann-cell segments with axon initially preserved
Wallerian degeneration, fragmented axons and myelin debrisSegmental myelin loss → impaired saltatory conduction / conduction block
Recovery depends on neuron survival, regrowth and target reinnervationSchwann remyelination may restore conduction when axons remain intact

Two diseases the lecturer specifically emphasizes

Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease (CMT) is a hereditary motor and sensory peripheral neuropathy. The lecture describes both demyelinating and axonal variants; presentation commonly begins in childhood/adolescence with slow progressive distal weakness and atrophy, foot drop, pes cavus, hammer toes, stocking-glove sensory loss and decreased ankle reflexes. The slides identify AD as common but recognize AR and X-linked forms.

Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acquired, usually postinfectious immune-mediated peripheral neuropathy; the lecturer emphasizes rapid segmental peripheral demyelination with ascending weakness, paralysis and possible respiratory failure. This time course is an important contrast with slowly progressive hereditary CMT. Respiratory weakness is a clinical emergency.

Other peripheral neuropathy etiologies listed by the professor include diabetes, vasculitis, uremia, B-vitamin/nutritional deficiency, alcohol, infections, compression, malignancy, and chemotherapy-related injury. The handout names taxanes, platinum-based drugs and vinca alkaloids as drug classes associated with chemotherapy-induced neuropathy; these are causes, not recommended treatments.

FIRST AID CONNECTIONFirst Aid 2025 (neurology disease table) associates CMT1A with PMP22 gene duplication; and acute inflammatory demyelinating GBS with reduced reflexes, possible albuminocytologic dissociation (high CSF protein with normal cell count), and treatment with IVIG or plasma exchange. These details supplement rather than replace the lecture.
CLINICAL CONNECTIONA patient with years of pes cavus, foot drop, distal muscle wasting and affected relatives suggests CMT. A patient developing days to weeks of ascending weakness after infection, especially with hyporeflexia and breathing problems, suggests GBS.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINTAfter peripheral nerve transection, what produces myelin ovoids, and what acts as the guidance path for regenerating axons?
Reveal answerThe distal axon/myelin undergo Wallerian degeneration and fragmentation into ovoids. Proliferating Schwann cells align in Bands of Büngner to guide proximal regrowing axons.
Learning objective 6

Spinal cord gray/white matter, neuropil and CNS glia

In transverse section, the spinal cord has centrally located butterfly-shaped gray matter, surrounding white matter, and a small central canal lined by ependymal cells. The anterior (ventral) horns contain large multipolar lower motor neurons, a signature structure in the professor’s H&E slides. Posterior (dorsal) horns contain local interneurons and second-order sensory neurons that process sensory signals, including pain and temperature. Thoracic and upper lumbar lateral horns contain preganglionic sympathetic neuron somata.

The surrounding white matter contains many ascending sensory and descending motor tracts, appearing pale/vacuolated on H&E where lipid myelin has been dissolved. Cross-sectional profiles of axons are prominent. Neuropil contains intermingled neuronal processes, glial processes, synapses and small vessels, particularly conspicuous in gray matter. The handout notes more extensive gray matter in the limb-related cervical/lumbar enlargements, whereas white matter volume grows from sacral toward cervical levels.

CNS glial cellWhat to recognize / remember
OligodendrocyteMyelinates segments on multiple CNS axons; contrast with one PNS axon internode per Schwann cell
AstrocyteStructural and metabolic support; blood–brain barrier regulation
MicrogliaResident CNS phagocytes/immune-surveillance cells
Ependymal cellSimple cuboidal/columnar epithelium lining ventricles and spinal central canal; participates in CSF homeostasis

How to read the slide: locate the anterior median fissure to establish the ventral side; identify centrally stained gray horns versus paler peripheral white matter, then point to the central canal. Zoom into anterior-horn gray matter to find the extremely large multipolar motor neuron with euchromatic nucleus and Nissl-rich soma.

DON’T MIX THESE UPThe first-order sensory neuron soma is in the dorsal-root ganglion; the dorsal horn contains central relay neurons (including second-order neurons). Slide 43 loosely labels dorsal-horn sensory cell bodies; the professor’s written handout clarifies their second-order role.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINTWhat distinguishes spinal-cord anterior-horn gray matter from peripheral nerve fascicles in H&E?
Reveal answerAnterior-horn gray contains conspicuous large multipolar motor-neuron cell bodies with Nissl substance. PNS nerve fascicles primarily contain axons, Schwann cells and connective tissues, not their parent neuron somata.
Learning objective 7

Sensory versus autonomic ganglia: identify them on histology

A ganglion is a PNS collection of neuron cell bodies with accompanying supportive glia and nerve fibers. The key practical distinction is whether the neuronal somata are pseudounipolar and tightly packed with complete satellite cuffs (sensory) or multipolar, more scattered and incompletely cuffed (autonomic).

Histologic clueDorsal-root / sensory ganglionAutonomic sympathetic or parasympathetic ganglion
Neuron typeLarge pseudounipolar primary sensory neuron somataMultipolar postganglionic neuron somata
Cell arrangementSomata usually tightly grouped, often toward peripherySomata more scattered among fibers and connective tissue
Satellite cellsDistinct, nearly complete ring around each somaScattered/incomplete or more flattened satellite covering
Local synapsesNo local synapse for primary sensory neuron relaySynapses present from preganglionic fibers onto postganglionic neurons
Characteristic examplesSpinal dorsal-root gangliaSympathetic chain ganglia or intramural/enteric myenteric ganglia

Three named ganglion locations in your practical

Dorsal-root ganglion: adjacent to a spinal sensory root; inspect large round pseudounipolar cells ringed by numerous satellite cell nuclei, plus myelinated nerve fascicles. Sympathetic ganglion: often near the vertebral column; ganglion neurons are widely spaced and may have off-center nuclei and brown lipofuscin granules. Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus: clusters of neuronal somata between the circular and longitudinal smooth muscle layers of the intestinal muscularis externa; the lecture calls these parasympathetic/intramural ganglia. The anatomic location between muscle layers is often the fastest identifier.

Lipofuscin is an age-related brown residual-body pigment in long-lived neurons; it can be prominent in ganglion somata. It is helpful for tissue recognition but does not uniquely identify sympathetic neurons.

PRACTICAL IDENTIFICATIONComplete satellite cuffs + packed round somata → sensory DRG. Scattered multipolar somata + less distinct satellite cuff → autonomic ganglion. Ganglion nestled between GI muscle layers → myenteric / Auerbach plexus.
SOURCE NOTEThe slide classifies myenteric ganglia under parasympathetic ganglia. They are anatomically part of the enteric nervous system and are subject to autonomic modulation; use the lecture’s label for the stated histology identification expectation while retaining the enteric distinction.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINTWhich three histology findings let you distinguish dorsal-root ganglion from autonomic ganglion?
Reveal answerDRG has densely packed large pseudounipolar somata, complete satellite cuffs and no local neuronal synapses. Autonomic ganglia have more scattered multipolar somata, less complete satellite coverings and ganglionic synapses.

MASTER THESE BEFORE MOVING ON

  1. Identify a neuron soma, its Nissl-rich cytoplasm, the Nissl-negative axon hillock and glial nuclei.
  2. Tell PNS Schwann myelin from unmyelinated Schwann ensheathment; recognize a node of Ranvier, and label endoneurium, perineurium and epineurium.
  3. Explain distal Wallerian degeneration and why Schwann cells/macrophages and Bands of Büngner matter for PNS regeneration.
  4. Differentiate slowly progressive hereditary CMT from acute immune GBS by mechanism, time course and clinical pattern.
  5. Identify ventral horn motor neurons, white versus gray matter and the histological distinctions between DRG, sympathetic and myenteric ganglia.

THE MOST USEFUL FIRST AID CONNECTIONS

  1. Schwann vs oligodendrocyte: one PNS internode/axon vs multiple CNS axons.
  2. Wallerian degeneration: distal axon/myelin disintegration, macrophage clearance; possible PNS regrowth guided by Schwann cells.
  3. CMT1A: PMP22 duplication linked to pes cavus, foot drop and distal atrophy.
  4. Guillain–Barré: ascending weakness and reduced reflexes, often following infection; IVIG or plasma exchange in classic acute demyelinating disease.
  5. Perineurium: fascicular covering forms the blood–nerve barrier.
